segments.t: At the casting studio, Samy takes the stage to pitch himself despite having zero acting experience. While the casting team reacts with amusement and skepticism, an assistant measures him for costume fitting. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.
Voilà, je me présente à vous.
Je n'ai pas d'expérience dans ce métier.
Mais je veux être comédien depuis toujours.
J'ai beaucoup de charisme naturel.
On le voit vraiment pour le rôle de Baptiste?
Je peux vous raconter une histoire drôle.
C'est une blague, ce garçon?
Je sais, c'est une idée de Gérard.
Quelle est votre pointure de chaussures?
Ma taille est quarante-deux en France.
Veuillez baisser les bras, s'il vous plaît.
Je prends vos mesures rapidement.
Ne rentrez pas le ventre pendant la mesure.
Merci beaucoup pour votre accueil.
Let's explore the conversation line by line and unpack the French phrases.
Voilà, je me présente à vous.
'Here I am, let me introduce myself to you.' The candidate opens his audition. The formal 'you' pronoun sets a courteous, professional distance around 'introduce'.
Je n'ai pas d'expérience dans ce métier.
'I have no experience in this profession.' The candidate admits his amateur background. The verb meaning 'have' pairs naturally with the noun for 'experience' in everyday conversation.
Mais je veux être comédien depuis toujours.
'But I have always wanted to be an actor.' The candidate expresses his lifelong passion. Notice how 'want' leads directly into the noun meaning 'actor'.
J'ai beaucoup de charisme naturel.
'I have a lot of natural charisma.' The candidate brags about his presence. The descriptive adjective for 'natural' agrees in gender and number with its noun.
On le voit vraiment pour le rôle de Baptiste?
'Are we really seeing him for the role of Baptiste?' The casting assistant whispers in disbelief. The verb meaning 'see' pairs naturally with the noun for 'role' in everyday conversation.
Je peux vous raconter une histoire drôle.
'I can tell you a funny story.' The candidate offers to entertain the room. The adjective meaning 'funny' takes its feminine form here to match the noun it describes.
C'est une blague, ce garçon?
'Is this boy a joke?' The assistant questions whethis the audition is serious. The key noun here means 'joke', anchored by its matching French article.
Je sais, c'est une idée de Gérard.
'I know, it is an idea from Gerard.' The colleague explains who suggested the candidate. The verb meaning 'know' pairs naturally with the noun for 'idea' in everyday conversation.
Quelle est votre pointure de chaussures?
'What is your shoe size?' The assistant turns to wardrobe details. The formal 'you' pronoun sets a courteous, professional distance around 'shoe size'.
Ma taille est quarante-deux en France.
'My size is forty-two in France.' The candidate states his measurements. The key noun here means 'size', anchored by its matching French article.
Veuillez baisser les bras, s'il vous plaît.
'Please lower your arms.' The assistant gives posing directions. The reflexive pronoun sits right in front of the verb for 'please', turning the action back onto the subject.
Je prends vos mesures rapidement.
'I am taking your measurements quickly.' The assistant works efficiently with the measuring tape. The verb meaning 'take' pairs naturally with the noun for 'measurements' in everyday conversation.
Ne rentrez pas le ventre pendant la mesure.
'Do not suck in your stomach during the measurement.' The assistant instructs him on natural posture. Notice the classic French sandwich negation wrapping right around 'suck in'.
Merci beaucoup pour votre accueil.

'Thank you very much for your welcome.' The candidate concludes politely. The formal 'you' pronoun sets a courteous, professional distance around 'thank you'. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more to lock in what you have learned.

Samy finishes his offbeat audition and measurement session with good humor. When you watch the episode, listen out for the expressions meaning 'introduce' and 'experience'. You'll catch them now. See you next time.
